  LARGE LOAD DEMAND                                 §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION

  LOWER COLORADO RIVER AUTHORITY' S COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSAL
                FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW §25.521

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       Lower Colorado River Authority (LCRA) submits these comments and executive summary

in response to Commission Staff's proposed new 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §25.521

relating to Large Load Demand Management Service in Project No. 58482.


                                   I.      INTRODUCTION

       LCRA appreciates the Commission's diligent work to implement Senate Bill 6, including

the provisions requiring development of a reliability service to competitively procure demand

reductions from large load customers to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency

condition. As more large loads come online in ERCOT, not only will these facilities impact

ERCOT operations, but they will also influence wholesale market outcomes. Consistent with the

Governor's directive to protect residential ratepayers from the costs of data center expansion,

LCRA urges the Commission to evaluate load price impacts and congestion on the system caused

by large loads. Therefore, in adopting rules to implement the new Large Load Demand

Management Service, the Commission should build into its regulatory framework an ongoing,

holistic review of the costs and benefits of large loads, including an economic analysis to evaluate

the impact large loads will have on the prices and congestion costs paid by all customers.

                                II.     RESPONSE TO QUESTIONS

        Question 1:
       Proposed subsection * (1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
       representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is subject
       to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management Services (LLDA/IS)
       obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available but not ultimately
       instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated some percentage
       of the market clearing price for the large load customer's availability to reduce demand
       during the LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate payment to the large
       load customer for their availability during LLDMS obligation period?
        Response:
        In previous comments submitted on LLDMS, LCRA was supportive of procuring the

service on an as-needed basis and establishing a budget to limit program costs.1 The proposal for

publication (PFP) effectively employs both ofthese measures and will avoid subjecting the market

to costly standby payments for rare emergency conditions. The PFP envisions a procurement

process that will seek to handle a targeted condition, that at most will be a month in advance of an

anticipated event but will most likely be requested just days ahead of an unexpected extreme

weather condition. LCRA cautions the Commission against reducing the payment to participants

of the service based on whether they were actually deployed or not. Potential participants in the

service are collectively weighing the costs that would be required to prepare for a deployment

(e.g., additional fuel purchases for onsite generation, increase in onsite personnel for emergency

operations, etc.) which should formulate the basis of their offers. If the benefit of participating in

the service (i.e., the market clearing price) is significantly reduced for a participant in the event of

a non-deployment, a large load may decide that participation is not worth the risk.

          Question 2:
        Proposed subsection *(4) imposes a maximum budget of S54 million in a calendar year.
        What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?
         Response:
         Target quantities for procurement should be tailored for each as-needed event and should

be linked to amounts that help return ERCOT back to normal operations. In this way, ERCOT

should limit each event' s impact on the annual spend limit. Notably, the $54 million annual budget

proposed is equivalent to the Firm Fuel Supply Service (FFSS) contract period budget. While it is

currently uncertain what amount of Large Load participation the LLDMS may receive, it is

unlikely that LLDMS will need to be procured frequently enough to align with the availability

hour requirement of the FFSS obligation period.2 This suggests that the $54 million annual spend

limit is higher than needed. The proper way to determine an appropriate budget would be to

analyze the universe of likely participants along with the probability of emergency events and their

related system needs. To gain insight into participation, the Commission should direct ERCOT to

conduct a participation survey to better understand the composition of load that might participate.

In the absence of this data, LCRA recommends that the annual spend limit be reduced to $27

million.

         Question 3:
        What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how
        far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?
         Response:
         LCRA supports the cadence set forth in subsection (d) of the PFP and finds that it is

appropriate for ERCOT to have a tiered set of forward-looking risk assessments.




2 The 2026-2027 contract period is November 15, 2026 through March 15, 2027 and contemplates 24-hour availability
for deployment needs (i.e., 2,880 hours). For LLDMS to reach an equivalent amount of procurement hours as is
required under an FFSS obligation, LLDMS would need to be procured 7.89 hours a day for each day ofthe year. This
scenario is extremely unlikely.

         Question 4:
        Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so, what
        limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?
        Response:
        Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 39.170 (b)(2) makes it clear that the service should

only be deployed during the event of an anticipated emergency condition. What is not clear is

ERCOT's interpretation of what should be considered an emergency condition~ under its Nodal

Protocols, so it is understandable to ask this question.

        ERCOT is currently planning to institute mitigation planszl to curtail groups ofLarge Loads

that do not currently meet voltage-ride through standards, and under certain scenarios, these groups

would subsequently cause transmission equipment to operate outside of defined limits. This

scenario could be classified as introducing a transmission emergency under the related definition

in § 25.521(b)(4) of the PFP, but it would be challenging to anticipate when it might occur. Under

this condition, it would be more appropriate for ERCOT to require these Large Loads to convert

to a Controllable Load Resource (CLR) construct, so the Security Constrained Economic Dispatch

model (SCED) could dynamically curtail the Large Loads to protect the system when issues arise.

This approach would be easier to manage and less costly to the market to implement. Procuring

groups of Large Loads that introduce this risk under an LLDMS construct would require open

ended procurement periods and issuance of manual deployments that would ultimately involve

ERCOT and Transmission Operator personnel to fully execute. If LLDMS is to be expanded to

mitigate transmission emergencies, the scenarios must be narrowly defined with clear exit

strategies in order to protect against domination of the annual spend limit.

                  III.     GENERAL COMMENTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Payments and charges - § 25.521(f)(1)

         As discussed in response to Question 1, the Commission should not limit the market

clearing price that a participant is eligible to receive. When procured for the service, the participant

should receive 100% of the market clearing price. The service should have robust claw back

penalties and should contemplate disqualification for pre-deployment and egregious performance

issues.5 Claw back penalties can be assessed on the normal settlement timeline as availability and

performance data is captured. Additionally, the $54 million dollar budget appears to be higher than

needed when comparing it to existing programs (i.e., FFSS) and infrequency oflikely procurement.

To gain insight into participation, the Commission should direct ERCOT to conduct a participation

survey to better understand the composition of load that might participate. In the absence of this

data, LCRA recommends that the annual spend limit be reduced to $27 million. LCRA offers the

following revisions to the PFP language to capture these thoughts:

After action reporting requirement - § 25.521(h)

       The data listed in this subsection will be useful in giving the market insights into

procurement and deployment events. LCRA offers the following revisions to enhance event

transparency:

(h)    After action reporting requirement. Not later than 60 days after an event in which

       ERCOT procures LLDMS, ERCOT must file a report with the commission detailing:

       (1)      the number of large load customers that submitted offers;

       (2)      the number of megawatts procured;

       (3)      the highest offer;

       (4)      the lowest offer;

                    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY TO LCRA'S COMMENTS


Consistent with the Governor's directive to protect residential ratepayers from the costs of data

center expansion, LCRA urges the Commission to evaluate load price impacts and congestion on

the system caused by large loads. Therefore, in adopting rules to implement the new Large Load

Demand Management Service, the Commission should build into its regulatory framework an

ongoing, holistic review of the costs and benefits of large loads, including an economic analysis

to evaluate the impact large loads will have on the prices and congestion costs paid by all

customers.

LCRA supports procuring the service on an as-needed basis and establishing a budget to limit

program costs.

LCRA cautions the Commission against reducing payments to participants based on whether

participants are actually deployed. If the financial benefit of participating is significantly reduced

in the event of a non-deployment, large loads may decide that participation is not worth the risk.

An appropriate budget should be determined by analyzing the universe of likely participants, the

probability of emergency events, and related system needs. To gain insight into participation, the

Commission should direct ERCOT to conduct a survey to better understand the composition of

load that might participate. In the absence of this data, LCRA recommends reducing the annual

spend limit to $27 million.

IfLLDMS is to be expanded to mitigate transmission emergencies, the scenarios must be narrowly

defined with clear exit strategies in order to protect against domination of the annual spend limit.
